suture

SOO-chur · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To suture is to stitch together the edges of a wound or surgical incision.

The surgeon explained to the nervous patient exactly how she would suture the incision once the operation was complete.

Example

After the fishing hook tore through his palm, the ship's cook used a sterilized needle to suture the cut himself, since the nearest hospital was two days away by boat.

Suture is a precise medical term for closing a wound with stitches -- it's more specific than a general word like 'treat.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stitch: Stitch is the everyday word for sewing something together with needle and thread — a torn sleeve, a loose button, a cut chin. To suture is the same act done clinically: a doctor closing the edges of a wound, using the precise term of hospitals and operating rooms. You stitch a hem; a surgeon sutures an incision.

sew: Sew means to join or repair almost anything with needle and thread, and it belongs mostly to the world of cloth — hems, quilts, costumes. Suture takes the same motion into medicine: it means stitching the edges of a wound or incision closed, and nothing else. All suturing is sewing; very little sewing is suturing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unstitch: to remove stitches, undoing what was sewn

tear: to rip or pull apart

Where it sits · how far the medical treatment goes — bandage → suture → operate on

bandage vs. suture: Bandage means to cover and protect a wound without necessarily closing it with stitches, a lighter step than suturing.

operate on vs. suture: Operate on means to perform full surgery, a far more extensive medical procedure than simply suturing a wound.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Suture comes from Latin sutura, 'a seam,' from suere, 'to sew' -- a surgeon who sutures a wound is literally sewing a seam in the skin. The same sewing root hides in the fashion word couture.

Use the root in a new word: couture

Use the root in a new word: couture: The designer's haute couture gowns were hand-stitched over hundreds of hours.
